claim: tRNAs shuttle between the nucleus and the cytoplasm
source: tRNAs are unique among various RNAs in that they shuttle between the nucleus and the cytoplasm, and their localization is regulated by nutrient conditions.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Takano et al., 2005; Shaheen and Hopper, 2005)

claim: tRNA localization is regulated by nutrient conditions
source: tRNAs are unique among various RNAs in that they shuttle between the nucleus and the cytoplasm, and their localization is regulated by nutrient conditions.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Ssa2p is a major cytoplasmic Hsp70 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
source: Here, we identified Ssa2p, a major cytoplasmic Hsp70 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, as a tRNA-binding protein whose deletion compromises nuclear accumulation of tRNAs upon nutrient starvation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Werner-Washburne et al., 1987

claim: Ssa2p is a tRNA-binding protein
source: Here, we identified Ssa2p, a major cytoplasmic Hsp70 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, as a tRNA-binding protein whose deletion compromises nuclear accumulation of tRNAs upon nutrient starvation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and label transfer assays in Figure 4

claim: Deletion of Ssa2p compromises nuclear accumulation of tRNAs upon nutrient starvation
source: Here, we identified Ssa2p, a major cytoplasmic Hsp70 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, as a tRNA-binding protein whose deletion compromises nuclear accumulation of tRNAs upon nutrient starvation.
evidence: Supported by FISH data in Figure 2A showing reduced nuclear accumulation in ssa2∆ mutant

claim: Ssa2p recognizes several structural features of tRNAs through its nucleotide-binding domain
source: Ssa2p recognizes several structural features of tRNAs through its nucleotide-binding domain, but prefers loosely-folded tRNAs, suggesting that Ssa2p has a chaperone-like activity for RNAs.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assays with NBD domain in Figure 6B and structural mutant analyses in Figure 5

claim: Ssa2p prefers loosely-folded tRNAs
source: Ssa2p recognizes several structural features of tRNAs through its nucleotide-binding domain, but prefers loosely-folded tRNAs, suggesting that Ssa2p has a chaperone-like activity for RNAs.
evidence: Supported by data showing enhanced binding to destabilized tRNA mutants in Figure 5B and preference for unmodified tRNAs in Figure 4E

claim: Ssa2p has a chaperone-like activity for RNAs
source: Ssa2p recognizes several structural features of tRNAs through its nucleotide-binding domain, but prefers loosely-folded tRNAs, suggesting that Ssa2p has a chaperone-like activity for RNAs.
evidence: Inferred from the preference for loosely-folded tRNAs and structural recognition properties

claim: Ssa2p binds Nup116, one of the yeast nucleoporins
source: Ssa2p also binds Nup116, one of the yeast nucleoporins.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data in Figure 7A

claim: Sis1p and Ydj1p are cytoplasmic co-chaperones for Ssa proteins
source: Sis1p and Ydj1p, cytoplasmic co-chaperones for Ssa proteins, were also found to contribute to the tRNA import.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of Hsp70 co-chaperones

claim: Sis1p and Ydj1p contribute to tRNA import
source: Sis1p and Ydj1p, cytoplasmic co-chaperones for Ssa proteins, were also found to contribute to the tRNA import.
evidence: Supported by FISH data in Figure 8 showing defects in sis1-151 and ydj1∆ mutants

claim: Cytoplasmic splicing of pre-tRNAs occurs in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
source: The first indication of nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling of tRNAs was the discovery of cytoplasmic splicing of pre-tRNAs in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Yoshihisa et al., 2003, 2007) in spite of the existence of small amounts of mature tRNAs in the nucleus (Sarkar and Hopper, 1998; Grosshans et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yoshihisa et al., 2003, 2007

claim: Small amounts of mature tRNAs exist in the nucleus
source: The first indication of nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling of tRNAs was the discovery of cytoplasmic splicing of pre-tRNAs in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Yoshihisa et al., 2003, 2007) in spite of the existence of small amounts of mature tRNAs in the nucleus (Sarkar and Hopper, 1998; Grosshans et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sarkar and Hopper, 1998; Grosshans et al., 2000

claim: Mature tRNAs move from the cytoplasm back into the nucleus
source: Subsequently, we and others demonstrated that mature tRNAs move from the cytoplasm back into the nucleus (Shaheen and Hopper, 2005; Takano et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shaheen and Hopper, 2005; Takano et al., 2005

claim: Nuclear import of tRNAs has been observed in mammals
source: Nuclear import of tRNAs has also been observed in mammals (Zaitseva et al., 2006; Shaheen et al., 2007; Miyagawa et al., 2012), suggesting that eukaryotic cells are equipped with mechanisms that allow bidirectional movement of tRNAs between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
evidence: Supported by citations to Zaitseva et al., 2006; Shaheen et al., 2007; Miyagawa et al., 2012

claim: Eukaryotic cells are equipped with mechanisms that allow bidirectional movement of tRNAs between the nucleus and the cytoplasm
source: Nuclear import of tRNAs has also been observed in mammals (Zaitseva et al., 2006; Shaheen et al., 2007; Miyagawa et al., 2012), suggesting that eukaryotic cells are equipped with mechanisms that allow bidirectional movement of tRNAs between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
evidence: Inferred from observations of tRNA import in multiple species

claim: Los1p/exportin-t is a primary export carrier of mature tRNAs in yeast, plants, and vertebrates
source: Los1p/exportin-t is considered as a primary export carrier of mature tRNAs in yeast, plants, and vertebrates (Arts et al., 1998; Hellmuth et al., 1998; Kutay et al., 1998; Sarkar and Hopper, 1998; Li and Chen, 2003; Park et al., 2005; Cook et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Arts et al., 1998; Hellmuth et al., 1998; Kutay et al., 1998; Sarkar and Hopper, 1998; Li and Chen, 2003; Park et al., 2005; Cook et al., 2009

claim: Yeast Los1p exports pre-tRNAs for cytoplasmic splicing
source: Besides, yeast Los1p exports pre-tRNAs for cytoplasmic splicing (Sarkar and Hopper, 1998; Yoshihisa et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sarkar and Hopper, 1998; Yoshihisa et al., 2003

claim: Msn5p/exportin-5 provides an alternative export pathway in yeast and mammals
source: Msn5p/exportin-5, another importin β homologue, provides an alternative export pathway in yeast and mammals (Bohnsack et al., 2002; Calado et al., 2002; Takano et al., 2005; Okada et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bohnsack et al., 2002; Calado et al., 2002; Takano et al., 2005; Okada et al., 2009

claim: Msn5p/exportin-5 is the main carrier of tRNAs in Drosophila
source: while Msn5p/exportin-5 is the main carrier of tRNAs in Drosophila (Büssing et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Büssing et al., 2010

claim: Los1p exports both newly synthesized and re-imported tRNAs
source: Los1p exports both newly synthesized and re-imported tRNAs while Msn5p exports only re-imported tRNAs (Eswara et al., 2009; Murthi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eswara et al., 2009; Murthi et al., 2010

claim: Msn5p exports only re-imported tRNAs
source: Los1p exports both newly synthesized and re-imported tRNAs while Msn5p exports only re-imported tRNAs (Eswara et al., 2009; Murthi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eswara et al., 2009; Murthi et al., 2010

claim: Export of spliced or mature tRNAs is coupled to a tRNA quality control step governed by nuclear aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases
source: In both cases, the export of spliced or mature tRNAs is coupled to a tRNA quality control step governed by nuclear aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (ARSs) to support efficient export of aminoacylated tRNAs (Lund and Dahlberg, 1998; Azad et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lund and Dahlberg, 1998; Azad et al., 2001

claim: Nuclear import of tRNAs can be blocked by depletion of intracellular ATP
source: Nuclear import of tRNAs can be blocked by depletion of intracellular ATP, indicating that the process is energy-dependent.
evidence: Supported by citation to Takano et al., 2005

claim: tRNA import is an energy-dependent process
source: Nuclear import of tRNAs can be blocked by depletion of intracellular ATP, indicating that the process is energy-dependent.
evidence: Inferred from ATP depletion blocking import

claim: tRNA import can operate in the absence of a gradient of GTP-bound Ran across the nuclear envelope
source: However, tRNA import can also operate even in the absence of a gradient of GTP-bound Ran across the NE, which is the main energy source for many macromolecular transport mediated by importin β (Takano et al., 2005; Grünwald et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Takano et al., 2005; Grünwald et al., 2011

claim: Both authentic tRNAs and some types of damaged tRNAs, such as CCA-less tRNAs, are imported into the nucleus
source: Both authentic tRNAs and some types of damaged tRNAs, such as CCA-less tRNAs, are imported (Takano et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takano et al., 2005

claim: Wybutosine formation on tRNA-PheGAA is initiated by nuclear Trm5p after cytoplasmic splicing of pre-tRNA-PheGAA
source: Wybutosine formation on tRNA-PheGAA is initiated by nuclear Trm5p after cytoplasmic splicing of pre-tRNA-PheGAA, indicating that nuclear import of a spliced intermediate precedes this modification (Ohira and Suzuki, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ohira and Suzuki, 2011

claim: Nuclear import of a spliced tRNA-PheGAA intermediate precedes wybutosine modification
source: Wybutosine formation on tRNA-PheGAA is initiated by nuclear Trm5p after cytoplasmic splicing of pre-tRNA-PheGAA, indicating that nuclear import of a spliced intermediate precedes this modification (Ohira and Suzuki, 2011).
evidence: Inferred from the nuclear location of Trm5p and cytoplasmic splicing

claim: Spliced tRNA species that are hypomodified and possess 5′- and 3′ extensions are retrograded into the nucleus to be repaired or degraded
source: In addition, spliced tRNA species but hypomodified and possessing 5′- and 3′ extensions, which are accidentally leaked from the nucleus in certain mutants, are retrograded into the nucleus to be repaired or degraded (Kramer and Hopper, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kramer and Hopper, 2013

claim: Mtr10p is an importin-β homologue originally identified as an import carrier for Npl3p
source: One possible import carrier is an importin-β homologue Mtr10p, which was originally identified as an import carrier for Npl3p, as mRNA-binding protein (Senger et al., 1998), and was shown to cause a defect in tRNA import when mutated (Shaheen and Hopper, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Senger et al., 1998; Shaheen and Hopper, 2005

claim: Mutation of Mtr10p causes a defect in tRNA import
source: One possible import carrier is an importin-β homologue Mtr10p, which was originally identified as an import carrier for Npl3p, as mRNA-binding protein (Senger et al., 1998), and was shown to cause a defect in tRNA import when mutated (Shaheen and Hopper, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shaheen and Hopper, 2005

claim: No evidence has been reported for tRNA binding by Mtr10p
source: Nevertheless, no evidence has been reported for tRNA binding by Mtr10p.
evidence: Based on absence of reports in the literature

claim: Depletion of various nutrients results in nuclear accumulation of tRNAs in S. cerevisiae
source: For instance, depletion of various nutrients, such as amino acids, phosphate, and glucose, results in nuclear accumulation of tRNAs in S. cerevisiae (Hurto et al., 2007; Whitney et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hurto et al., 2007; Whitney et al., 2007

claim: Alteration of tRNA localization affects translation efficiency of certain mRNAs that encode enzymes for amino acid biosynthesis
source: Indeed, such alteration of tRNA localization affects translation efficiency of certain mRNAs that encode enzymes for amino acid biosynthesis, suggesting that retrieval of tRNAs from the cytosol has, at least, a regulatory role (Chu and Hopper, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chu and Hopper, 2013

claim: Retrieval of tRNAs from the cytosol has a regulatory role
source: Indeed, such alteration of tRNA localization affects translation efficiency of certain mRNAs that encode enzymes for amino acid biosynthesis, suggesting that retrieval of tRNAs from the cytosol has, at least, a regulatory role (Chu and Hopper, 2013).
evidence: Inferred from effects on translation efficiency

claim: Signal transduction pathways mediated by PKA and TOR facilitate tRNA transport regulation in yeast
source: To alter the tRNA balance, signal transduction pathways mediated by PKA and TOR, but not Gcn2p, facilitate this transport regulation in the yeast (Whitney et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whitney et al., 2007

claim: Gcn2p does not facilitate tRNA transport regulation in yeast
source: To alter the tRNA balance, signal transduction pathways mediated by PKA and TOR, but not Gcn2p, facilitate this transport regulation in the yeast (Whitney et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whitney et al., 2007

claim: tRNA export carriers Los1p and Msn5p are not phosphorylated in vivo according to nutrient status
source: Although several kinases were shown to act on the regulation of tRNA transport, tRNA export carriers Los1p or Msn5p are not phosphorylated in vivo according to the nutrient status, and they are not substrates for PKA in vitro (Pierce et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pierce et al., 2014

claim: Los1p and Msn5p are not substrates for PKA in vitro
source: Although several kinases were shown to act on the regulation of tRNA transport, tRNA export carriers Los1p or Msn5p are not phosphorylated in vivo according to the nutrient status, and they are not substrates for PKA in vitro (Pierce et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pierce et al., 2014

claim: Tef1p (eEF1A) is a tRNA binding protein
source: As summarized in Figure 1C, Tef1p (eEF1A in the yeast) and Eno2p (enolase) were identified, both of which are already known as tRNA binding proteins (Nagata et al., 1984; Entelis et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nagata et al., 1984; Entelis et al., 2006 and identification in Figure 1C

claim: Eno2p (enolase) is a tRNA binding protein
source: As summarized in Figure 1C, Tef1p (eEF1A in the yeast) and Eno2p (enolase) were identified, both of which are already known as tRNA binding proteins (Nagata et al., 1984; Entelis et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nagata et al., 1984; Entelis et al., 2006 and identification in Figure 1C

claim: Mammalian Hsp70 (Hsc70) interacts with an AU-rich element
source: Among the proteins associated with the tRNA-resin in an ATP-sensitive manner, Ssa1p and/or Ssa2p, two major cytosolic Hsp70s with highly homologous sequences, were of interest because mammalian Hsp70 (Hsc70) was shown to interact with an AU-rich element, which defines short-lived mRNAs (Henics et al., 1999; Laroia et al., 1999; Lu et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Henics et al., 1999; Laroia et al., 1999; Lu et al., 2006

claim: The yeast ssa1 mutant strain exhibits defective degradation of mRNAs possessing AU-rich elements
source: In addition, the yeast ssa1 mutant strain exhibits defective degradation of mRNAs possessing this AU-rich element (Duttagupta et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duttagupta et al., 2003

claim: Only immunoprecipitates of Ssa2p-FLAG in the absence of ATP contained tRNA-ProUGG at levels above background
source: When analyzed by Western blotting with the anti-FLAG antibody and by Northern blotting with an anti-mature tRNA-ProUGG probe (Figure 1D), only immunoprecipitates of Ssa2p-FLAG in the absence of ATP contained tRNA-ProUGG at levels above background, indicating that the Ssa protein we identified as a tRNA-binding protein was Ssa2p.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Neither ssa1∆ nor ssa2∆ mutants exhibit altered tRNA localization in a los1∆ msn5∆ background under normal growth conditions
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, neither the ssa1∆ nor ssa2∆ mutants exhibits altered tRNA localization in a los1∆ msn5∆ background.
evidence: Supported by FISH data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: ssa2∆ mutant cells re-established the tRNA gradient across the nuclear envelope after energy depletion
source: Furthermore, ssa2∆ mutant cells re-established the tRNA gradient across the NE after energy depletion like the other strains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, bottom row).
evidence: Supported by FISH data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Neither Ssa2p nor Ssa1p plays a major role in tRNA import under normal growth conditions
source: These results indicate that neither Ssa2p nor Ssa1p plays a major role in tRNA import under normal growth conditions.
evidence: Inferred from lack of effect in los1∆ msn5∆ background experiments

claim: Wild-type and ssa1∆ cells accumulated both tRNA-ProUGG and tRNA-iMet in the nucleus under amino acid starvation conditions within 2 hr
source: While the wild-type and ssa1∆ cells accumulated both tRNA-ProUGG and tRNA-iMet in the nucleus under these conditions within 2 hr, relatively lower amounts of tRNA-ProUGG and tRNA-iMet were observed in the ssa2∆ nuclei (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by FISH data in Figure 2A

claim: Relatively lower amounts of tRNA-ProUGG and tRNA-iMet were observed in the ssa2∆ nuclei under amino acid starvation
source: While the wild-type and ssa1∆ cells accumulated both tRNA-ProUGG and tRNA-iMet in the nucleus under these conditions within 2 hr, relatively lower amounts of tRNA-ProUGG and tRNA-iMet were observed in the ssa2∆ nuclei (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by FISH data in Figure 2A

claim: All examined tRNAs (tRNA-LysCUU, tRNA-LysUUU, and tRNA-TyrGUA) were apparently affected by ssa2∆ mutation
source: We also examined three other tRNA species, tRNA-LysCUU, tRNA-LysUUU, and tRNA-TyrGUA, in FISH, and found that all the tRNAs were apparently affected by ssa2∆ mutation while the effects of ssa1∆ mutation were not obvious if any (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by FISH data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The effects of ssa1∆ mutation on tRNA accumulation were not obvious
source: We also examined three other tRNA species, tRNA-LysCUU, tRNA-LysUUU, and tRNA-TyrGUA, in FISH, and found that all the tRNAs were apparently affected by ssa2∆ mutation while the effects of ssa1∆ mutation were not obvious if any (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by FISH data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The average NAI of tRNA-ProUGG in wild-type cells was 1.52 ± 0.09 under starvation conditions
source: While the average nuclear accumulation indices (NAIs), rations of nuclear FISH signals against cytosolic signals, of tRNA-ProUGG in the wild-type, ssa1∆, and ssa2∆ cells were nearly equal when the cells were grown in YPD, the NAIs of these strains became 1.52 ± 0.09, 1.58 ± 0.10, and 1.14 ± 0.25, respectively, when the cells were starved, revealing an apparent difference between tRNA import in the wild-type cells and that in the ssa2∆ cells.
evidence: Supported by quantitative FISH data in Figure 2A

claim: The average NAI of tRNA-ProUGG in ssa1∆ cells was 1.58 ± 0.10 under starvation conditions
source: While the average nuclear accumulation indices (NAIs), rations of nuclear FISH signals against cytosolic signals, of tRNA-ProUGG in the wild-type, ssa1∆, and ssa2∆ cells were nearly equal when the cells were grown in YPD, the NAIs of these strains became 1.52 ± 0.09, 1.58 ± 0.10, and 1.14 ± 0.25, respectively, when the cells were starved, revealing an apparent difference between tRNA import in the wild-type cells and that in the ssa2∆ cells.
evidence: Supported by quantitative FISH data in Figure 2A

claim: The average NAI of tRNA-ProUGG in ssa2∆ cells was 1.14 ± 0.25 under starvation conditions
source: While the average nuclear accumulation indices (NAIs), rations of nuclear FISH signals against cytosolic signals, of tRNA-ProUGG in the wild-type, ssa1∆, and ssa2∆ cells were nearly equal when the cells were grown in YPD, the NAIs of these strains became 1.52 ± 0.09, 1.58 ± 0.10, and 1.14 ± 0.25, respectively, when the cells were starved, revealing an apparent difference between tRNA import in the wild-type cells and that in the ssa2∆ cells.

claim: Deletion of either SSA3 or SSA4 had no impact on tRNA accumulation under starvation conditions
source: Deletion of either of the other two SSA genes, SSA3 and SSA4, which are only expressed under stress conditions, had no impact on tRNA accumulation under starvation conditions (Figure 2A, table).
evidence: Supported by quantitative FISH data in Figure 2A table

claim: SSA3 and SSA4 are only expressed under stress conditions
source: Deletion of either of the other two SSA genes, SSA3 and SSA4, which are only expressed under stress conditions, had no impact on tRNA accumulation under starvation conditions (Figure 2A, table).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of SSA gene expression

claim: Simultaneous deletion of SSA1 and SSA2 genes did not result in an obvious additive effect on tRNA accumulation
source: When the effect of simultaneous deletion of SSA1 and SSA2 genes was examined, the double deletion did not result in the obvious additive effect (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by FISH data in Figure 3

claim: The ssa2∆ GAL7p-MTR10 double mutant showed an additive decrease in the signal intensity of nuclear tRNA-ProUGG
source: The double mutant showed an additive decrease in the signal intensity of nuclear tRNA-ProUGG (Figure 2B, ssa2Δ mtr10↓), and signal quantification revealed that the average NAI of the starved double mutant (0.87 ± 0.04) was clearly below those observed for the mtr10 and ssa2Δ single mutants (0.98 ± 0.04 and 1.11 ± 0.07, respectively), and was far below that observed for the wild type strain (1.30 ± 0.10).
evidence: Supported by quantitative FISH data in Figure 2B

claim: The average NAI of the starved ssa2∆ mtr10 double mutant was 0.87 ± 0.04
source: The double mutant showed an additive decrease in the signal intensity of nuclear tRNA-ProUGG (Figure 2B, ssa2Δ mtr10↓), and signal quantification revealed that the average NAI of the starved double mutant (0.87 ± 0.04) was clearly below those observed for the mtr10 and ssa2Δ single mutants (0.98 ± 0.04 and 1.11 ± 0.07, respectively), and was far below that observed for the wild type strain (1.30 ± 0.10).
evidence: Supported by quantitative FISH data in Figure 2B

claim: The probability that the NAIs of the mtr10 single and mtr10 ssa2∆ double mutants were the same was only 0.037
source: Student's t-test indicated that the probability that the NAIs of the mtr10 single and mtr10 ssa2∆ double mutants were the same was only 0.037 while the difference between those of the mtr10 single and mtr10 ssa1∆ double mutants was not significant (p = 0.92).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of FISH data

claim: The difference between NAIs of the mtr10 single and mtr10 ssa1∆ double mutants was not significant (p = 0.92)
source: Student's t-test indicated that the probability that the NAIs of the mtr10 single and mtr10 ssa2∆ double mutants were the same was only 0.037 while the difference between those of the mtr10 single and mtr10 ssa1∆ double mutants was not significant (p = 0.92).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of FISH data

claim: Ssa2p and Mtr10p act independently in parallel pathways for tRNA import under starvation conditions

claim: A slight but distinct increase in the nuclear signals of both Ssa1p and Ssa2p was observed when cells were incubated in SD+Ura, Ade

evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2C

claim: Both Ssa1p and Ssa2p received radioactivity from 32P-labeled (AUUU)5 RNA but not from (ACCC)5 RNA

claim: Label transfer from (AUUU)5 RNA to Ssa proteins was dependent on UV-irradiation and sensitive to ATP
source: Both Ssa1p and Ssa2p received radioactivity from 32P-labeled (AUUU)5 RNA but not from (ACCC)5 RNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and label transfer was dependent on UV-irradiation and sensitive to ATP.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: No label transfer was observed when BSA was used as a control protein
source: Besides, no label transfer was observed when BSA was used as a control protein.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data

claim: Both Ssa1p and Ssa2p received radioactivity from 32P-labeled tRNA-ProUGG in an ATP-sensitive manner
source: Both Ssa1p and Ssa2p received radioactivity from 32P-labeled tRNA-ProUGG in an ATP-sensitive manner (Figure 4A,B) with only a marginal difference between the capacity of the two Ssa proteins to recognize the tRNA in vitro.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 4A,B

claim: There is only a marginal difference between the capacity of Ssa1p and Ssa2p to recognize tRNA in vitro
source: Both Ssa1p and Ssa2p received radioactivity from 32P-labeled tRNA-ProUGG in an ATP-sensitive manner (Figure 4A,B) with only a marginal difference between the capacity of the two Ssa proteins to recognize the tRNA in vitro.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 4A,B

claim: Both Ssa1p and Ssa2p received radioactivity efficiently from CCA-less tRNA-ProUGG
source: As shown in Figure 4A, both Ssa1p and Ssa2p received radioactivity efficiently from the CCA-less tRNA.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 4A

claim: Ssa proteins bind tRNAs irrespective of their anticodon loop structure
source: Label transfer with an intron-containing pre-tRNA was also performed and revealed that Ssa proteins bind tRNAs irrespective of their anticodon loop structure.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay with pre-tRNA

claim: In vitro-transcribed tRNA-ProUGG efficiently competed with radioactive tRNA-ProUGG for label transfer
source: When the specificity of tRNA recognition by Ssa proteins was tested by competition experiments with short RNAs, chemical amounts of in vitro-transcribed tRNA-ProUGG efficiently competed with the radioactive amount of tRNA-ProUGG for label transfer (Figure 4C, lanes 'tRNA') while only limited competition was observed with single-stranded homo-oligo-ribonucleotides (A30, U30, and G30) or a double-stranded homo-oligomer (A-U)30.
evidence: Supported by competition assay data in Figure 4C

claim: Only limited competition was observed with single-stranded homo-oligo-ribonucleotides (A30, U30, and G30) or a double-stranded homo-oligomer (A-U)30
source: When the specificity of tRNA recognition by Ssa proteins was tested by competition experiments with short RNAs, chemical amounts of in vitro-transcribed tRNA-ProUGG efficiently competed with the radioactive amount of tRNA-ProUGG for label transfer (Figure 4C, lanes 'tRNA') while only limited competition was observed with single-stranded homo-oligo-ribonucleotides (A30, U30, and G30) or a double-stranded homo-oligomer (A-U)30.
evidence: Supported by competition assay data in Figure 4C

claim: Ssa proteins specifically recognize tRNAs in an ATP-sensitive manner via a mechanism that is not mediated through the 3′ end adenosine or the anti-codon loop of tRNAs
source: These results indicate that Ssa proteins specifically recognize tRNAs in an ATP-sensitive manner via a mechanism that is not mediated through the 3′ end adenosine or the anti-codon loop of tRNAs, and that these properties resemble those observed in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from CCA-less tRNA binding and pre-tRNA binding data

claim: Label transfer efficiencies were variable among different isoacceptor tRNAs
source: When different isoacceptor tRNAs were used as donors for radioactivity, the label transfer efficiencies were variable.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 4D

claim: tRNA-ProUGG was a potent substrate for label transfer

evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 4D

claim: tRNA-PheGAA was a very poor substrate for label transfer irrespective of 32P-labeled nucleotides used for in vitro transcription
source: In particular, tRNA-ProUGG was a potent substrate for label transfer while tRNA-PheGAA was a very poor substrate irrespective of 32P-labeled nucleotides used for in vitro transcription (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 4D

claim: All tRNAs, including tRNA-PheGAA, competed with radiolabeled tRNA-ProUGG for label transfer
source: Competition experiments revealed that all tRNAs, including tRNA-PheGAA, competed with radiolabeled tRNA-ProUGG for label transfer even though their competition efficiencies were variable (Figure 4E).

claim: Unmodified tRNA-ProUGG was a more potent competitor than the fully-modified tRNA
source: It should be noted that unmodified tRNAs-ProUGG was a more potent competitor than the fully-modified tRNA.
evidence: Supported by competition assay data in Figure 4E

claim: Various tRNAs are recognized by Ssa proteins with different affinities
source: These results indicate that various tRNAs are recognized by Ssa proteins with different affinities and that certain nucleotide positions of a tRNA molecule may offer the sites for this recognition.

claim: Ssa proteins recognize differences in structural characteristics between unmodified and fully-modified tRNAs
source: The above results also show that Ssa proteins recognize differences in structural characteristics between unmodified and fully-modified tRNAs.
evidence: Inferred from differential competition by modified vs unmodified tRNAs

claim: An antisense oligonucleotide against the 5′ half of tRNA-ProUGG inhibited label transfer only when hybridized with the substrate by denaturation and annealing

evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 5A

claim: Heat denaturation and quick cooling of the tRNA substrate alone did not affect label transfer efficiency
source: Heat denaturation and quick cooling of the tRNA substrate alone did not affect label transfer efficiency, probably due to rapid refolding of the tRNA molecule.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 5A

claim: Introduction of G18A and U54C mutations, which disrupts the interaction between the D and TΨC loops, reduced label transfer efficiency
source: Introduction of G18A and U54C mutations, which disrupts the interaction between the D and TΨC loops, reduced label transfer efficiency.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 5B

claim: Destabilization of the acceptor stem by introducing G69C or G68C substitutions resulted in higher label transfer efficiency
source: On the other hand, destabilization of the acceptor stem by introducing G69C or G68C substitutions resulted in higher label transfer efficiency, while a C67G mutation reduced the efficiency of label transfer.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 5B

claim: A C67G mutation reduced the efficiency of label transfer
source: On the other hand, destabilization of the acceptor stem by introducing G69C or G68C substitutions resulted in higher label transfer efficiency, while a C67G mutation reduced the efficiency of label transfer.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 5B

claim: Positive and negative effects induced by acceptor stem mutations were minimized by compensatory mutations
source: Both of these positive and negative effects induced by acceptor stem mutations were minimized by compensatory mutations (Figure 5B, gray bars).
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 5B

claim: Replacement of the acceptor stem of human tRNA-LeuAAG with acceptor-like stems from unstable tRNA-like noncoding RNAs enhanced recognition by Ssa2p
source: Indeed, replacement of the acceptor stem of human tRNA-LeuAAG with acceptor-like stems from unstable tRNA-like noncoding RNAs (mouse MALAT1-associated cytoplasmic small RNA and MEM β RNA) enhanced recognition by Ssa2p (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 5C

claim: Single replacement of the G1-C71 Watson-Crick pair with the non-Watson-Crick pair (G1•U71) in tRNA-ArgUGC enhanced recognition by Ssa2p
source: This is also true even for single replacement of the G1-C71 Watson-Crick pair with the non-Watson-Crick pair (G1•U71) in tRNA-ArgUGC.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 5C

claim: Ssa proteins recognize the overall structure of tRNAs, and prefer tRNAs with a destabilized acceptor stem but with a stable core structure
source: These results suggest that Ssa proteins recognize the overall structure of tRNAs, and prefer tRNAs with a destabilized acceptor stem but with a stable core structure.
evidence: Inferred from mutational analysis of tRNA structure

claim: RCMLA addition did not inhibit, but rather moderately enhanced label transfer from tRNA-ProUGG
source: As shown in Figure 6A, RCMLA addition did not inhibit, but rather moderately enhanced label transfer from tRNA-ProUGG.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 6A

claim: tRNAs are not recognized by Ssa proteins through their SBDs
source: These results suggest that tRNAs are not recognized by Ssa proteins through their SBDs.
evidence: Inferred from lack of competition by protein substrate RCMLA

claim: GST-NBD and GST-NBD-SBD fusions of Ssa1p and Ssa2p received radioactivity from tRNA-ProUGG while fusions without NBD did not
source: GST-NBD and GST-NBD-SBD fusions of Ssa1p and Ssa2p received radioactivity from tRNA-ProUGG while fusions without NBD did not, indicating that the NBD plays an essential role in tRNA recognition by Ssa proteins (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 6B

claim: The NBD plays an essential role in tRNA recognition by Ssa proteins
source: GST-NBD and GST-NBD-SBD fusions of Ssa1p and Ssa2p received radioactivity from tRNA-ProUGG while fusions without NBD did not, indicating that the NBD plays an essential role in tRNA recognition by Ssa proteins (Figure 6B).
evidence: Inferred from domain deletion analysis

claim: The label transfer efficiencies of the GST-NBD and GST-NBD-SBD proteins were apparently lower than that of full-length Ssa proteins
source: It should be noted that the label transfer efficiencies of the GST-NBD and GST-NBD-SBD proteins were apparently lower than that of full-length Ssa proteins (Figure 6B, the left most 6 lanes).
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 6B

claim: The CVD appears to contribute to the efficient recognition of tRNAs by the NBD
source: Therefore, the CVD appears to contribute to the efficient recognition of tRNAs by the NBD.
evidence: Inferred from reduced efficiency of NBD-only constructs

claim: Mutations F66L and K69Q enhanced tRNA binding
source: Mutations affecting efficiency of ATP hydrolysis and its activation, namely F66L and K69Q, enhanced tRNA binding while those compromising nucleotide binding/exchange (G199D) reduced the binding (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 6C

claim: Mutation G199D reduced tRNA binding
source: Mutations affecting efficiency of ATP hydrolysis and its activation, namely F66L and K69Q, enhanced tRNA binding while those compromising nucleotide binding/exchange (G199D) reduced the binding (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 6C

claim: Mutations E228Q and D229N in the NBD caused virtually no changes in tRNA binding
source: Those mutations in the NBD that alter structural response to the nucleotide state (E228Q, D229N) caused virtually no changes in the tRNA binding.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 6C

claim: Particular residues in the NBD are responsible for tRNA recognition by Ssa proteins
source: These results indicate that particular residues in the NBD are responsible for tRNA recognition by Ssa proteins, and that the structural features of the ATP/ADP binding state are important for the tRNA binding.
evidence: Inferred from mutational analysis of NBD residues

claim: The structural features of the ATP/ADP binding state are important for tRNA binding
source: These results indicate that particular residues in the NBD are responsible for tRNA recognition by Ssa proteins, and that the structural features of the ATP/ADP binding state are important for the tRNA binding.
evidence: Inferred from effects of mutations affecting ATP hydrolysis and binding

claim: The NBDs of Ssa1p and Ssa2p responded differently to mutations F66L and K69Q
source: Interestingly, the NBDs of Ssa1p and Ssa2p responded differently to these mutations; the Ssa1p-NBD responded more strongly to F66L and K69Q than the Ssa2p-NDB.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 6C

claim: Mutations E173S and T201A only caused negative effects on the Ssa2p-NBD
source: More prominently, E173S and T201A, which affect the nucleotide binding/exchange, only caused negative effects on the Ssa2p-NBD, suggesting that these differences in in vitro-binding of tRNAs might be the reason why Ssa2p but not Ssa1p is responsible for nuclear import of tRNAs in vivo.
evidence: Supported by label transfer assay data in Figure 6C

claim: Differences in in vitro-binding of tRNAs might be the reason why Ssa2p but not Ssa1p is responsible for nuclear import of tRNAs in vivo
source: More prominently, E173S and T201A, which affect the nucleotide binding/exchange, only caused negative effects on the Ssa2p-NBD, suggesting that these differences in in vitro-binding of tRNAs might be the reason why Ssa2p but not Ssa1p is responsible for nuclear import of tRNAs in vivo.
evidence: Speculated based on differential mutational effects

claim: Both Ssa proteins specifically interacted with GST-Nup116(165–715)p, but not with GST-Nup100(1–640)p or with GST-Nsp1(1–601)p
source: Interestingly, both Ssa proteins specifically interacted with GST-Nup116(165–715)p, but not with GST-Nup100(1–640)p or with GST-Nsp1(1–601)p.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data in Figure 7A

claim: Ssa proteins can interact with the NPC through binding to certain Nups, such as Nup116p
source: These results suggest that Ssa proteins can interact with the NPC through binding to certain Nups, such as Nup116p.
evidence: Inferred from specific interaction with Nup116p

claim: Peripheral fluorescence on glutathione-beads was observed only when beads coated with GST-Nup116(165–715)p were incubated with fluorescent tRNA in the presence of Ssa proteins
source: Peripheral fluorescence on the glutathione-beads were observed only when the beads coated with GST-Nup116(165–715)p were incubated with the fluorescent tRNA in the presence of Ssa proteins (Figure 7B), while no such peripheral signal was seen in the absence of Ssa proteins and when GST-coated beads were used.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 7B

claim: Ssa2p drives interaction of tRNAs to the NPC
source: These results support the idea that Ssa2p drives interaction of tRNAs to the NPC.
evidence: Inferred from tRNA-Nup116p binding assay results

claim: Both the sis1-151 and ydj1∆ mutants showed an apparent defect in the nuclear accumulation of tRNAs under starvation conditions
source: As shown in Figure 7, both the sis1-151 and ydj1∆ mutants showed an apparent defect in the nuclear accumulation of tRNAs under starvation conditions while the zuo1∆ mutant cells were able to accumulate tRNAs in the nucleus.
evidence: Supported by FISH data in Figure 8

claim: The zuo1∆ mutant cells were able to accumulate tRNAs in the nucleus under starvation conditions
source: As shown in Figure 7, both the sis1-151 and ydj1∆ mutants showed an apparent defect in the nuclear accumulation of tRNAs under starvation conditions while the zuo1∆ mutant cells were able to accumulate tRNAs in the nucleus.
evidence: Supported by FISH data in Figure 8

claim: Ssb1p and Ssb2p are excluded from the nucleus and stay in the cytoplasm
source: This is consistent with the finding that Ssb1p and Ssb2p are excluded from the nucleus and stay in the cytoplasm while Ssa1p and Ssa2p shuttles between the two compartments (Shulga et al., 1999), and indicates that DnaJ proteins specific for Ssa1p and Ssa2p are required for tRNA import.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shulga et al., 1999

claim: Ssa1p and Ssa2p shuttle between the nucleus and cytoplasm
source: This is consistent with the finding that Ssb1p and Ssb2p are excluded from the nucleus and stay in the cytoplasm while Ssa1p and Ssa2p shuttles between the two compartments (Shulga et al., 1999), and indicates that DnaJ proteins specific for Ssa1p and Ssa2p are required for tRNA import.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shulga et al., 1999

claim: DnaJ proteins specific for Ssa1p and Ssa2p are required for tRNA import
source: This is consistent with the finding that Ssb1p and Ssb2p are excluded from the nucleus and stay in the cytoplasm while Ssa1p and Ssa2p shuttles between the two compartments (Shulga et al., 1999), and indicates that DnaJ proteins specific for Ssa1p and Ssa2p are required for tRNA import.
evidence: Inferred from defects in sis1 and ydj1 mutants but not zuo1 mutant

claim: snl1∆ did not affect nuclear accumulation of tRNAs under starvation conditions
source: In contrast to the case of sis1-151 and ydj1∆, snl1∆ did not affect nuclear accumulation of tRNAs under starvation conditions, indicating that Snl1p is not involved in this process.
evidence: Supported by FISH data in Figure 8

claim: Snl1p is not involved in tRNA import
source: In contrast to the case of sis1-151 and ydj1∆, snl1∆ did not affect nuclear accumulation of tRNAs under starvation conditions, indicating that Snl1p is not involved in this process.
evidence: Inferred from lack of effect in snl1∆ mutant

claim: The ATPase cycle of Ssa2p plays an essential role in tRNA import
source: Nevertheless, the effects of the sis1 and ydj1 mutations support the assumption that the ATPase cycle of Ssa2p plays an essential role in tRNA import.
evidence: Inferred from involvement of DnaJ co-chaperones that regulate ATPase activity

claim: Ssa2p acts as an import carrier of tRNAs across the NPC
source: Although there are several other possibilities for involvement of the Ssa2p chaperone system in tRNA import, from the collective pieces of experimental results, we primarily propose that Ssa2p acts as an import carrier of tRNAs across the NPC.
evidence: Proposed based on collective experimental evidence

claim: The ssa2∆ phenotype is only obvious under starvation conditions
source: Since the ssa2∆ phenotype is only obvious under starvation conditions, Ssa2p may provide a secondary pathway to accommodate high demand for the tRNA import under these conditions.
evidence: Supported by FISH data showing effects only under starvation

claim: Ssa2p may provide a secondary pathway to accommodate high demand for tRNA import under starvation conditions
source: Since the ssa2∆ phenotype is only obvious under starvation conditions, Ssa2p may provide a secondary pathway to accommodate high demand for the tRNA import under these conditions.
evidence: Speculated based on condition-specific phenotype

claim: The Ssa2p pathway may confer a regulatory capability to the tRNA nuclear import, responding to growth conditions
source: In other words, the Ssa2p pathway may confer a regulatory capability to the tRNA nuclear import, responding to growth conditions like the case of tRNA export (Murthi et al, 2010; Huang and Hopper, 2014; Pierce et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculated based on analogy to tRNA export regulation

claim: Ssa2p has some contribution to basal nuclear import of tRNAs under normal conditions by co-operating with the Mtr10p pathway
source: We speculate that Ssa2p also has some contribution to basal nuclear import of tRNAs under normal conditions by co-operating with the Mtr10p pathway, and that quantitative regulation of the Ssa2p pathway, but not complete on-and-off, enables enhancement of nuclear import under starvation conditions.
evidence: Speculated based on experimental observations
